notes:
Here are the verse-by-verse notes on 2 Samuel 11, drawn from the sources I was able to access.

---

## 2 Samuel 11 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### v. 1 — David stays home from war

**"In the spring, at the time when kings march out to war"** — Literally "at the return/revolution of the year." Spring (the month Nisan/Abib, roughly March–April) was the standard season for military campaigns in the ancient Near East because the winter rains had ceased and food was available for men and horses (Gill; Precept Austin cites Walton's IVP Background Commentary). Ellicott notes this refers back to 2 Samuel 10:14 — Joab had spent the rainy season in Jerusalem and now returned to Ammon.

**"David sent out Joab … but David remained in Jerusalem"** — This is the hinge of the whole tragedy. David should have been at the battle; in the previous chapter (2 Sam 10:17) he personally led the forces. Gill remarks, "it would have been well for him if he had gone forth with the army himself, then the sin he fell into would have been prevented." Precept Austin calls the word **"but"** "one of the most strategic terms of contrast in David's life … a hinge word … that would mark a change of direction that would affect the remainder of David's life." Warren Wiersbe (cited by Precept Austin) notes that David had been advised by his leaders not to engage actively in warfare (2 Sam 21:15–17), but he could still have been with his troops to give moral leadership. Enduring Word says David's staying home "merely provided an opportunity for the long-standing lack of sexual restraint and indulgence of passion to display itself." Multiple sources cite the proverbs "idle hands are the devil's playground" and Spurgeon's warning about the danger of idleness.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-11/
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-samuel-11-commentary
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-samuel-11.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-11.html

**The deeper root** — Enduring Word and Precept Austin (citing Chuck Swindoll) both stress that David's problem began years earlier when he took multiple wives in defiance of Deuteronomy 17:17 ("he shall not multiply wives for himself, lest his heart turn away"). Swindoll identifies three "breaches" in David's seawall: (1) polygamy and lust, (2) vulnerability from success and pride, (3) indulgence and idleness.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-11/
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-samuel-11-commentary

---

### v. 2 — David sees Bathsheba bathing

**"David got up from his bed and strolled around on the roof"** — Ellicott explains this was late afternoon, after the customary midday siesta; the flat roof was the coolest and pleasantest part of an Eastern house. The Hebrew verb for "walked" suggests David paced restlessly back and forth (Enduring Word). Gill notes that David was "indulging himself more than he used to do to sloth and luxury." The palace on Mount Zion looked down into the open courts of houses in the lower city, and Bathsheba's bathing place was "probably entirely concealed from every other point of observation than the roof of the palace, from which no harm was suspected" (Ellicott).

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-11.html
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-11/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-samuel-11.html

**"He saw a woman bathing — a very beautiful woman"** — Enduring Word is emphatic: "David's sin was not in seeing Bathsheba. It was unlikely that he expected or planned to see her. David's sin was in choosing to keep his eyes on an alluring image after the sight came before his eyes." The commentary adds that David's many wives did not satisfy his lust because "you can't satisfy lusts of the flesh … It wasn't so much that David wanted Bathsheba, it was that he would not be satisfied with what God gave him." Gill says the woman was "of a fine shape and good complexion, and comely countenance; all which were incentives to lust, at which his eye was attracted to, and his heart was ensnared."

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-11/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-samuel-11.html

**Possible immodesty on Bathsheba's part** — Enduring Word raises the possibility: "Though it was evening and apparently the time when most people were asleep, it is possible (even likely) that she knew that her bath was visible from the roof of the palace." However, it immediately adds: "Any possible immodesty on Bathsheba's part did not excuse David's sin."

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-11/

---

### v. 3 — David inquires about the woman

**"David sent and inquired about the woman"** — Gill suggests that if David had any honorable intention, he might have been thinking of marriage if she were unmarried, "but it would have been better for him not to have inquired at all, and endeavoured to stifle the motions raised in him at the sight of her." Enduring Word says David "could have ended the temptation by leaving the scene … Instead, David put himself into a more tempting situation."

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-samuel-11.html
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-11/

**"Bathsheba, the daughter of Eliam and the wife of Uriah the Hittite"** — Enduring Word notes this revealed that she came from a notable family: Eliam was one of David's mighty men (2 Sam 23:34), and her grandfather was Ahithophel, one of David's chief counselors (2 Sam 15:12). Uriah was also one of David's thirty mighty men (2 Sam 23:39). Ellicott comments: "David had now given rein to his guilty passion so far that the knowledge of Bath-sheba's being a married woman, and the wife of one of his chief warriors, does not check him." Enduring Word adds: "David should have received the news of the woman's identity as a warning … In taking Bathsheba, David sinned against Uriah, Eliam, and Ahithophel — each man was close and important to David." Ellicott notes that "Bath-sheba" is spelt "Bath-shua" in Chronicles, and "Eliam" becomes "Ammiel" — the same name with component parts transposed, meaning "God's people" / "people of God."

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-11.html
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-11/

---

### v. 4 — David commits adultery with Bathsheba

**"David sent messengers to get her … he slept with her"** — The verb "took" is the key interpretive point. Ellicott says explicitly: "This does not imply the use of violence." Gill likewise: "not by force, but through persuasion." Enduring Word, citing Keil & Delitzsch: "In the expression 'he took her, and she came to him' there is no intimation whatever that David brought Bathsheba into his palace through craft or violence, but rather that she came at his request without any hesitation, and offered no resistance to his desires. Consequently Bathsheba is not to be regarded as free from blame." It also cites Clarke: "We hear nothing of her reluctance, and there is no evidence that she was taken by force." Ellicott adds that Bathsheba "appears from the narrative of 1 Kings 2:13-22, to have been a woman of little discretion, and now yielded to David's will without resistance, perhaps flattered by the approach of the king." Gill notes: "she consenting to it, being prevailed upon, and drawn into it through the greatness and goodness of the man, which might make the sin appear the lesser to her."

**A note on differing views:** The traditional reading above (Gill, Ellicott, Enduring Word, Keil & Delitzsch) sees Bathsheba as at least partly complicit. Some modern interpreters argue that David's royal position made any "consent" impossible and that the power differential makes this effectively an act of coercive rape — but this argument was not found in the accessible pages from the specified sites. Enduring Word does title a video "Did King David Rape Bathsheba?" suggesting the debate exists even in conservative circles.

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-11.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-samuel-11.html
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-11/

**"(Now she had just purified herself from her uncleanness)"** — All commentators agree this refers to the ceremonial cleansing after menstruation (Lev 15:19). It confirms Bathsheba was not pregnant before the encounter with David, and it explains why she was bathing (ritual purification, not merely refreshment). Gill adds that it also meant "she was the more apt for conception." Enduring Word notes this detail proves the child was David's.

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-11.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-samuel-11.html
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-11/

**David's culpability** — Enduring Word says: "If David had thought about all this, he would have seen the cost … an unwanted pregnancy, the murder of a trusted friend, a dead baby, a daughter raped by his son, one son murdered by another, a civil war." The Ligonier devotional says David "apparently goes temporarily insane over her" and "gives every appearance of a man whose conscience is seared."

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-11/
- https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/davids-great-sin

---

### v. 5 — Bathsheba tells David she is pregnant

**"I am pregnant"** — This simple message (just two words in Hebrew, per Enduring Word) was an urgent appeal. Keil & Delitzsch (cited by Enduring Word) says it "involved an appeal to him to take the necessary steps to avert the evil consequences of the sin, inasmuch as the law required that both the adulterer and adulteress should be put to death (Lev 20:10)." Ellicott similarly: "Because her sin must now become known, and by the Law adulterers must both be punished with death." Gill adds that she feared "the outcries of the people … the rage and jealousy of her husband … and the death which by the law she was guilty of, even to be stoned with stones."

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-11/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-11.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-samuel-11.html

---

### vv. 6–8 — David's first attempt to cover his sin

**"Send me Uriah the Hittite"** — Enduring Word says: "When David heard the disastrous news of Bathsheba's pregnancy, he should have used it as a prompting to repent. Instead, David did what most unrepentant sinners do: he tried to hide his sin." David's plan was to have Uriah sleep with his wife so the child would appear to be his. Ellicott: "By calling for Uriah and treating him with marked consideration, he thought to establish a friendly feeling on his part, and then by sending him to his wife to have it supposed that the child, begotten in adultery, was Uriah's own." Clarke (cited by Enduring Word): "At this time he had no design of the murder of Uriah, nor of taking Bath-sheba to wife."

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-11/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-11.html

**"Go down to your house and wash your feet"** — A idiomatic expression for going home to refresh and rest (Gill). David also sent a "gift" after him — lit. "a present" or "a mess of meat" (Ellicott), likely a choice dish to honor Uriah and perhaps to encourage marital intimacy.

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-11.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-samuel-11.html

---

### vv. 9–11 — Uriah refuses to go home

**"Uriah slept at the door of the palace"** — Ellicott says it is "quite unnecessary to suppose that Uriah had any suspicion of what had been done. His conduct and language is simply that of a brave, frank, generous-hearted soldier." Gill, however, notes that some speculate he may have heard rumors from the guards about his wife being summoned to the palace. Trapp (cited by Enduring Word) says: "It is like he smelt something." Either way, all sources agree Uriah's refusal was providentially ordered to expose David's sin.

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-11.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-samuel-11.html
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-11/

**"The ark and Israel and Judah are dwelling in tents … How can I go to my house?"** — Uriah shows greater loyalty and self-denial than David. Enduring Word: "Uriah is a good example of how Christians should conduct themselves as fellow-soldiers in the spiritual battle." Ellicott notes the ark was apparently taken to the battlefield, a custom known from 1 Samuel 4:4. Ellicott adds: "This noble answer of Uriah should have stung David to the quick, but his conscience was so deadened by his sin that the only effect was to lead him to yet baser means of concealment." The Ligonier devotional remarks: "On this occasion, Uriah was far more noble and godly than David, who was not bothered that Israel's soldiers were at risk while he was at home enjoying himself."

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-11.html
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-11/
- https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/david-does-evil-in-eyes-of-lord

**"As surely as you live, and as your soul lives, I will not do such a thing!"** — Uriah swears an oath, which Gill says was "to prevent any further solicitations from the king, or his wife unto it."

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-samuel-11.html

---

### vv. 12–13 — David's second attempt: getting Uriah drunk

**"Stay here one more day … David got Uriah drunk"** — David now compounds his sin. Gill: "this was another sin of David's, done in order to make him forget his oath and vow." Enduring Word: "David was drunk with lust when he slept with Bathsheba; he hoped making Uriah drunk with wine would bring the same result." Yet even drunk, Uriah's resolve held. Ellicott: "Uriah's resolve was so strong that it still governed his conduct while in this almost irresponsible condition." All sources see God's providential hand in this: "the Lord no doubt working upon his mind and disinclining him to it" (Gill).

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-samuel-11.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-11.html
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-11/

---

### vv. 14–17 — David arranges Uriah's death

**"David wrote a letter to Joab and sent it with Uriah"** — The trusted soldier carries his own death warrant. Ellicott: "The brave soldier is made the bearer of his own death-warrant, and his well-known valour for his king is to be the means of accomplishing his destruction." Enduring Word: "David trusted the integrity of Uriah so much that he made him the unwitting messenger of his own death sentence." Gill draws a parallel to the Greek myth of Bellerophon, suggesting the biblical story may have inspired it. Meyer (cited by Enduring Word) imagines Joab saying, "This master of mine can sing psalms with the best; but when he wants a piece of dirty work done, he must come to me."

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-11.html
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-11/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-samuel-11.html

**"Put Uriah at the front of the fiercest battle; then withdraw from him"** — Ellicott notes that the order to "withdraw" was **not** carried out: "Perhaps Joab thought it would make the stratagem too evident, or perhaps it was impracticable. At all events, the consequence was that others were slain with Uriah, and thus a larger blood-guiltiness fell upon David." Enduring Word: "David commanded Joab to arrange Uriah's death. Though it was hidden by the raging battle, Uriah was murdered just as surely as if David killed him in his own home." Trapp: "David was better while a servant than when a king; for being a servant, he feared to kill Saul his adversary, but becoming a king, he basely slew his most faithful friend and dutiful subject."

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-11.html
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-11/

**V. 17 — "Uriah the Hittite also died"** — Enduring Word traces the snowball: "One unrepentant sin snowballs: lust became adultery, adultery became deception, and deception became murder."

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-11/

---

### vv. 18–25 — Joab sends word to David

**Joab's preemptive instructions (vv. 20–21)** — Joab anticipated David's anger at the tactical blunder of drawing too close to the city wall. He references the story of Abimelech (Judges 9:50–57), who was killed by a woman dropping a millstone from a wall at Thebez. Ellicott explains Joab's strategy: "Joab anticipated David's anger at his apparent rashness, and charged the messenger, when he should observe it, to mention Uriah's death. This was not likely to awaken any suspicion in the messenger, as it would appear to him rather as an effort on Joab's part to throw the blame from himself upon Uriah as the leader of the assaulting party." Gill says Joab "knew very well it would pacify the king's wrath, and was the agreeable news he wanted to hear."

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-11.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-samuel-11.html

**David's reply (v. 25): "the sword devours one as well as another"** — A proverb about the fortunes of war. Enduring Word: "David said it to his own guilty conscience as much as he said it to Joab." Ellicott paraphrases the thought: "though Uriah was a brave hero whom we could ill spare, yet in the fortune of war we cannot choose who shall fall." Gill contrasts David's hardened conscience here with the tender conscience that once troubled him for merely cutting Saul's robe.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-11/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-11.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-samuel-11.html

---

### vv. 26–27 — David marries Bathsheba

**"When Uriah's wife heard … she mourned for him"** — Ellicott says the usual mourning period was seven days (Gen 50:10; 1 Sam 31:13); a widow's might have been longer but "was doubtless, under the circumstances, made as short as was consistent with decency." Enduring Word suggests Bathsheba "may have been partly relieved, knowing that the crisis of her pregnancy from David was now averted."

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-11.html
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-11/

**"David had her brought to his house, and she became his wife and bore him a son"** — Ellicott notes several months have passed since the beginning of David's sin, "and as yet his conscience had not brought him to a sense of what he had done, nor had the prophet Nathan been sent to him." Ellicott also notes that "during all this time David was not only the civil ruler of his people, but also the head of the theocracy, the great upholder of the worship and the service of God, and his psalms were used as the vehicle of the people's devotion." The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary notes: "All looked well on the surface, but it is known that there was great strife and turmoil in David's heart, as revealed in Psalms 51, 32."

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-11.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/2-samuel-11.html

**"But the thing that David had done was evil in the sight of the LORD"** — This is the first explicit mention of God in the entire chapter (Enduring Word). The Ligonier devotional translates more literally: "David did what was evil in the eyes of the Lord." Enduring Word: "This is the first mention of God in the chapter. God witnessed every event and read the intent of every heart, but His displeasure was only implied until now." John Piper (Desiring God) calls this "one of the most understated sentences of the Bible." All Protestant traditions are united here: God saw everything, and David's elaborate cover-up fooled no one in heaven. Ellicott asks why God left David so long without confronting him, and offers: "one obvious reason is, that this sin might be openly fastened upon him beyond all possibility of denial by the birth of the child." He adds that David's conscience was almost certainly at work, "oppressing him with that sense of unconfessed and unforgiven sin which prepared him at last for the visit of Nathan."

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-11/
- https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/david-does-evil-in-eyes-of-lord
- https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/a-broken-and-contrite-heart-god-will-not-despise
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-11.html

**Spurgeon on David's delayed repentance** — Cited by Enduring Word: "When there is the most necessity for confession, there is often the greatest tardiness in making it. It was so in David's case … I think I can see why he could not have gone straight away from the sin to confession, for the sin prevented the confession — the sin blinded the eye, stultified the conscience, and stupefied the entire spiritual nature of David." Spurgeon also observed: "Though we mourn over David's sin, yet we thank God that it was permitted, for if he had not so fallen he had not been able to help us when we are conscious of transgression."

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-11/

---

## Summary of Denominational Distinctives

**Baptist** — Gill's Exposition and Garner-Howes both emphasize the "sin will find you out" principle (Num 32:23), David's personal accountability, and the progression of sin when unconfessed. Spurgeon (Baptist, cited in Enduring Word) stresses the danger of delayed confession and the merciful purpose of recording David's fall for the help of future penitents. John Piper (Reformed Baptist, Desiring God) emphasizes that David's forgiveness was immediate upon confession but tied to the future work of Christ: "God sees from the time of David down the centuries to the death of his Son, Jesus Christ, who would die in David's place."

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-11/
- https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/a-broken-and-contrite-heart-god-will-not-despise
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-samuel-11.html

**Reformed** — Ligonier stresses God's sovereignty in not letting David remain in sin: "But God will not let his son remain in sin. He sends Nathan." It also emphasizes the "seared conscience" and the warning that "failure to remember that God sees everything leads very quickly to sin."

- https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/davids-great-sin
- https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/david-does-evil-in-eyes-of-lord

**Pentecostal/Charismatic** — Enduring Word (David Guzik) provides the most extensive practical application: guarding the eyes, the danger of idle time, the snowball effect of unconfessed sin, the failure of polygamy to satisfy, and the importance of immediate confession. The approach is warmly devotional and aimed at personal holiness.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-11/

**Anglican** — Ellicott's older commentary (1878) provides historical, linguistic, and cultural background with pastoral reflection: "His fall, as St. Augustine has said, should put upon their guard those who have not fallen, and save from despair those who have." Ellicott is gentler toward Bathsheba's possible indiscretion while firmly placing the weight of guilt on David.

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-11.html
